state.case_summary:
A 67-year-old man with hypertension, dyslipidaemia, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, active smoking (35 pack-years), a family history of ischaemic heart disease, and prior percutaneous coronary interventions (2008, 2017, 2022) for non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction presented with Canadian Cardiovascular Society Class III angina. A recent exercise stress test induced angina at 50 W without ECG changes. On admission, he appeared anxious; the physical examination was unremarkable. A 12-lead ECG showed normal sinus rhythm, Q waves in lead III, and biphasic T waves in leads III and aVF. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 65% without regional wall-motion abnormalities. Coronary angiography demonstrated patent stents in the circumflex artery, non-significant disease in the left anterior descending artery, and significant ostial right coronary artery stenosis with in-stent restenosis in the mid-segment, which was treated with three drug-eluting stents. After transfer to the intensive care unit, he complained of worsening chest pain; ECG showed ST-segment elevation in leads V1–V3, and echocardiography remained normal. A second angiogram showed patent stents but subocclusion of the right coronary postero-lateral branch, successfully treated with balloon angioplasty, relieving his pain. Shortly thereafter, he developed recurrent sustained polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation requiring seven external shocks and 15 minutes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Post-resuscitation ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm with persistent precordial ST-segment elevation and new QTc prolongation to 500 ms. Repeat echocardiography revealed akinesia of all apical segments, later extending to mid-segments, hyperkinesia of the basal segments, and severely reduced LVEF of 35%, leading to suspicion of takotsubo syndrome.
